title: Buying the Laptop
subtitle: A day of shopping for electronics, and four verbs that English refuses to let you swap.
description: A B1 reading and listening text following a day spent buying tech, written to practise say, speak, talk and tell, with vocabulary and comprehension exercises.
passage: I had been putting off buying a new laptop for about a year, and last Saturday the old one finally made the decision for me by refusing to turn on. So I spent the day shopping, which I do not enjoy, and came home having spent more than I meant to, which is the usual outcome.

The first shop was the good one. I told the assistant what I actually needed — something that could handle video editing without sounding like it was about to take off — and she listened, which is rarer than it should be. She spoke about three machines in turn and was honest that the most expensive one was more than I needed. Then she said something that decided it: “This one will still be fast in four years. That one won't.” I said I would take it.

The second shop was less good. I had gone in to look at smart home devices, and the assistant talked at me for ten minutes about a security system I had already said I did not want. When I told him I was only interested in a thermostat, he told me the thermostat was on sale, which turned out to be true, so the visit was not wasted. I bought the thermostat and left.

After that I looked online, because I have learned that nobody in a shop is going to tell you that the same software is forty per cent cheaper on the manufacturer's own website. It was. I bought an office suite and, in a moment of weakness I am still thinking about, a smartwatch that had been reduced twice.

In the evening I called my friend Marcus, who knows more about this than I do, and told him what I had bought. He said the laptop was a good choice and asked why I had bought the watch. I said I did not entirely know. We talked for half an hour about whether any of it was necessary, which is a conversation we have had before and will have again.
The next morning the new laptop arrived and did in ninety seconds what the old one had stopped being able to do at all. I have not spoken to Marcus about the watch since.

vocabulary.definition: the way something finally turns out
to be capable of dealing with a demanding task
to leave the ground, said of an aircraft
to speak to someone without listening to them
the company that makes a product
to lower the price of something
a set of programs for writing, spreadsheets and presentations

exercises.title: Understanding the Text
exercises.instructions: Answer from the sense of the story, including its dry humour.

items.prompt: What finally made the writer replace the laptop?
options: A sale that was about to end
The old one stopped turning on
items.explanation: “The old one finally made the decision for me by refusing to turn on” — after a year of putting it off.

items.prompt: Why does the writer call the first assistant good?
options: She listened, and was honest that the most expensive machine was more than he needed
She sold him the most powerful option
items.explanation: The praise is for listening and for talking him out of spending more — “rarer than it should be”.

items.prompt: Which sentence actually decided the purchase?
options: That the machine could handle video editing
That the price had been reduced twice
That this one would still be fast in four years and the other would not
items.explanation: The writer marks it out: “Then she said something that decided it.”

items.prompt: What was wrong with the second assistant?
options: He gave inaccurate information about the thermostat
He talked at the writer about a product the writer had already refused
He refused to apply the sale price
items.explanation: “Talked at me” is the phrase — speaking without listening. His information about the sale was in fact true.

items.prompt: Why does the writer check online prices?
options: Because shop staff will not tell you the same software is much cheaper elsewhere
Because online shops always have better stock
Because the shops had sold out
items.explanation: “Nobody in a shop is going to tell you that the same software is forty per cent cheaper on the manufacturer's own website.”

items.prompt: What does the writer imply about the smartwatch?
options: That it was the best purchase of the day
That it was bought impulsively and is regretted
That it was needed for work
items.explanation: “A moment of weakness I am still thinking about” — and the final line confirms it: he has not raised it with Marcus since.

items.prompt: What is the joke in the last sentence?
options: That Marcus was proved wrong about the laptop
That the writer is quietly avoiding the subject he could not defend
items.explanation: The laptop was a good decision and gets reported; the watch was not, so the conversation is dropped. The joke is left for the reader to finish.

exercises.title: Say, Speak, Talk or Tell?
exercises.instructions: The rough rules: you SAY words. You TELL a person something. You TALK to someone about a topic. You SPEAK when the tone is more formal, or about languages.

items.prompt: I ___ the assistant what I actually needed.
items.explanation: Tell takes a person straight after it: tell someone something. “Said the assistant” would be wrong here.

items.prompt: Then she ___ something that decided it.
items.explanation: Say takes the words, not the listener. To use tell you would need a person: “told me something”.

items.prompt: The assistant ___ at me for ten minutes about a system I did not want.
items.explanation: Talk AT someone is deliberately different from talk TO someone — it means speaking without listening.

items.prompt: We ___ for half an hour about whether any of it was necessary.
items.explanation: Talk is the verb for a two-way conversation about a topic.

items.prompt: She ___ about three machines in turn.
items.explanation: Speak about is slightly more formal than talk about, and fits a professional explaining options.

items.prompt: Nobody is going to ___ you the software is cheaper online.
items.explanation: There is a person (“you”) immediately after the verb, so it must be tell.

items.prompt: I have not ___ to Marcus about the watch since.
items.explanation: Speak TO someone. Talk to would also be natural here; say and tell would not fit this structure.

exercises.title: True or False?
exercises.instructions: Decide whether each statement matches the story.

items.statement: The first assistant persuaded him to buy the most expensive laptop.
items.explanation: False — she was honest that it was more than he needed.

items.statement: The second assistant's claim about the sale was untrue.
items.explanation: False — it “turned out to be true, so the visit was not wasted”. His fault was not listening.

items.statement: The writer bought the software in a shop.
items.explanation: False — he bought it online, where it was forty per cent cheaper.
True — “he said the laptop was a good choice”, and then asked about the watch.

discussion: The writer praises an assistant for talking him out of spending more. Has anyone ever done that for you?
What is the difference between someone talking TO you and talking AT you? Describe an example.
“A moment of weakness I am still thinking about.” What was yours?
Is it reasonable to check a shop's prices online while standing in the shop?
Write about 120 words about something you bought recently, using say, tell, talk and speak at least once each.
